analysis.one_liner: Extends overtime pay, paid sick days, written contracts, breaks, and anti-discrimination protections to the nation's roughly 2.2 million domestic workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 9, 2025, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would extend basic workplace rights to domestic workers — nannies, house cleaners, home health and personal care aides — who have been largely excluded from federal labor law. It would end the exemption that denies live-in domestic workers overtime pay, require written contracts, guarantee paid sick days, meal and rest breaks, and 72-hour notice of schedule changes, extend workplace anti-discrimination law (Title VII) to domestic workers, ban retaliatory firing and immigration threats, and create enforcement tools including a national hotline, a standards board, and grants for outreach. It would also temporarily increase federal Medicaid matching funds to help pay for the new requirements in home care. It has only been referred to committee and has not advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 2.2 million domestic workers in the United States — nannies, housekeepers, cooks, home health and personal care aides — would gain overtime pay for live-in work, paid sick days, written employment agreements, meal and rest breaks, predictable scheduling with 72-hour notice, termination notice with lodging or severance for live-in workers, and access to anti-discrimination protections under Title VII. About 9 in 10 are women, disproportionately women of color and immigrants, and the bill's findings note domestic workers are three times as likely as other workers to live in poverty. Families and individuals who receive home care would also benefit from more stable, better-trained workers and lower turnover.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic workers, mostly women of color and immigrants

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Fair Labor Standards Act provision that has exempted live-in domestic workers from overtime pay, so they would earn time-and-a-half for hours over 40 a week.
Requires written, plain-language employment agreements covering pay, hours, duties, and grievance processes, and bans forced arbitration and noncompete terms in those agreements.
Grants up to 56 hours of paid sick time a year (1 hour earned per 30 worked), usable for the worker's own or a family member's illness, medical care, or safe time after domestic violence.
Requires 72 hours' notice of schedule changes and pay for canceled or shortened shifts, plus the right to request temporary schedule changes for personal events like caregiving.
Guarantees meal and rest breaks, privacy protections (no monitoring in living quarters or bathrooms), and bans wage deductions for the employer's cash shortages or breakages.
Amends Title VII of the Civil Rights Act so domestic workers can sue for workplace discrimination and harassment.

Requires 48-hour written termination notice plus 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance for live-in workers, guarantees communication access, creates a federal hotline, an interagency enforcement task force, a Domestic Employee Standards Board, and grants for community outreach.

analysis.who_pays: Households that employ domestic workers would bear new costs and paperwork: written agreements, sick leave accrual, overtime for live-in workers, scheduling-notice obligations, and severance or 30-day lodging after terminating a live-in worker. Medicaid-funded home care programs would face higher labor costs, which the bill offsets only temporarily through an increased federal Medicaid match. Employers could no longer use arbitration clauses, nondisclosure terms, or immigration-status threats against these workers.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes real compliance burdens on ordinary households, not just agencies: written agreements, 72-hour scheduling notice, sick-leave accrual, and meal and rest breaks would apply to families employing nannies or home aides, raising costs of in-home care.

Medicaid-funded home and community-based care services provided by domestic employees would become more expensive; the bill responds with only a temporary increase in the federal Medicaid match (Sec. 401), so states and families could face cost pressure after it ends.
Bans on arbitration, noncompete, and nondisclosure terms in domestic-work agreements (Sec. 110(d)(2)) reduce employer options and could discourage some families from hiring help.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to a low-paid, mostly female workforce are large and concrete: overtime pay for live-in workers, paid sick days, written contracts, break rights, and civil-rights coverage, with enforcement teeth and anti-retaliation protections. The costs are real but modest in context: households that employ help would face new paperwork, scheduling rules, and payroll obligations, and Medicaid-funded home care would cost governments more unless the temporary federal match covers it. Exceptions for shared living arrangements and abuse allegations soften the burden, but the bill would be hard for small households and informal employers to navigate, and enforcement against millions of individual households is genuinely difficult. On balance the bill's gains for workers and for care quality outweigh its administrative costs.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill on December 9, 2025, read it twice, and sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has remained with no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 9, 2025 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral is the only action the bill has received; there is no record of a hearing, markup, floor vote, or companion House action.
The bill's 17 cosponsors are all Democrats or allied independents, led by Senator Gillibrand, giving it no recorded Republican support in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody has gained yet. Domestic workers remain without the bill's protections, and nothing has changed for employers either. If the bill never reaches the Senate floor, households and agencies that rely on informal, unprotected domestic labor will be better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; employers of domestic help if it stalls

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 9, 2025 and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: 16 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent cosponsor (incl. Sanders, Warren, Fetterman, Duckworth, Booker, Klobuchar, Markey, Merkley)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; all 17 cosponsors are Democrats or allied independents.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors are Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a committee with no recorded action.

industries.industry: Domestic workers (nannies, home health and personal care aides, housekeepers)
industries.note: About 2.2 million workers, disproportionately immigrant women and women of color, would gain overtime pay, paid sick days, written contracts, breaks, and discrimination protections they have historically been excluded from. Their median wage is about $16.58 an hour and they are three times as likely as other workers to live in poverty.

Millions of ordinary families employing nannies or aides would face new paperwork, scheduling notice, and pay obligations, raising the cost of in-home care. At the same time, families relying on aides would benefit from more stable, trained, and less frequently quitting workers.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and Medicaid-funded home care
industries.note: The bill raises labor standards for Medicaid-funded home care services while offering a temporary increase in the federal Medicaid matching rate to cover the added wage costs (Secs. 307, 401). Agencies would bear compliance costs, offset in part by federal funds and by lower turnover.

The bill bars platforms from penalizing workers who communicate directly with clients instead of through the platform's app, and extends wage-deduction protections to platform workers, limiting a control mechanism platforms currently use.

analysis.trajectory: The bill faces long odds. It has no Republican cosponsors, sits in the Senate HELP Committee with no scheduled hearing, and would likely also need 60 votes to clear a Senate filibuster. A first-term bill referred to committee late in a session with only same-party support rarely reaches the floor; unless it gains bipartisan support or is attached to a larger package, it will probably die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress.
